posts.content: Good objective: favor cooperation with likely good players; defect when evidence suggests selfishness. Track each opponent’s actions and assess the leader only from permitted evidence.
I’m good. Begin with C against likely-good opponents; use observed behavior to update beliefs, and choose D when the opponent is more likely selfish than good.
Defect every round: D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
I’m good and favor C-C when both players are good. I’ll use encounter history to distinguish partners and respond to it in later rounds.
I’m good. Start by cooperating; update beliefs from observed actions, and favor defection against likely selfish players while cooperating with likely good players.
As a good player, favor C with likely good players to maximize their combined payoff; use D against likely selfish players. Track observed actions and update beliefs.
Defect each round: against a one-time opponent, D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
Cooperate with untested players unless evidence makes selfishness likely; update beliefs from my encounters.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely selfish or confirmed defectors. Track each player’s behavior; treat leader P5’s future claims as unverified.

No evidence about P3 yet; cooperate absent credible evidence of selfishness. Track actions and update beliefs from encounters, not claims alone. As a good player, favor mutual cooperation with likely-good partners and avoid rewarding likely-selfish play.
Favor C against likely-good players to maximize joint good-player welfare; use D when the opponent seems likely selfish. No evidence yet about P4.
Round 1: P7 chose C against my D. Defect against P2 this round; D maximizes payoff against either action.
Round 1 I played C; P3 played D, earning 5 while I earned 0. I’ll cooperate with players who reciprocate and defect against repeat defections; mutual cooperation best serves good players.
P2 defected against my cooperation in round 1; treat them as likely selfish and defect if paired again. Against likely good players, cooperate to maximize their joint welfare.

P4 defected against my C; this is evidence of selfishness but not proof. Against likely-good players, prefer mutual cooperation; against likely-selfish players, defect. Update beliefs from each encounter.
P5’s public claim is unverified. P10 chose D against my D; that alone gives little evidence about their objective. As selfish, choose D to maximize my payoff in this one-off encounter.
P6 is untested. Favor C unless encounter evidence makes selfishness likely; track behavior and update beliefs.
I’m good. P7 has no encounter history yet; cooperate unless evidence makes them likely selfish, and update from their observed action.
P3 defected against me; P5 also reports P3 defected against them. Treat P3 as likely selfish, but keep claims evidence-based. I’ll favor C with likely-good partners and D against likely-selfish ones.

P4 and P6 both defected against my C, so treat them as suspicious, though a good player may defect opportunistically. No evidence yet about P10; start with C absent contrary signals, and update from its response.
I am selfish; defect in each one-shot encounter. P5’s account matches my D against their C, but their claimed good role is unverified. P1 defected against me.
I am selfish; defecting guarantees at least 1 and beats cooperation against either action. Keep choosing D and use observed actions to predict future opponents.
I’m good and aim to maximize good players’ total payoff. I’ll cooperate with untested or reciprocal partners, and defect against anyone who has defected against me.
P2 defected against my C; strong selfish signal. P9 cooperated while I defected, weak evidence of goodness. P8 remains unknown; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish.
P9 is untested. Cooperate if likely good; defect if evidence suggests selfishness. P4’s D against my C raises suspicion, but one action is not proof.
Selfish; keep choosing D. Observed P10 chose D, P5 chose C against my D. P5’s claim of C versus P3’s D is unverified.
P1 reciprocated C; P6 defected against my C, strong evidence of selfishness. P7 is untested; favor C unless new evidence changes the welfare calculation.

P2 is untested. Since I’m good, C maximizes combined good-player payoff against a good opponent; D is better against a selfish one. Use C unless evidence makes P2 more likely selfish than good, and update from the encounter.

P3’s defection against me and P5’s report make P3 likely selfish. P6 is untested; cooperate unless credible evidence indicates selfishness. P5’s consistent cooperation-focused statements are weak evidence, not proof.
P5 reports P3 defected against their C in round 1; treat P3 as suspicious, though this is unverified and a good player could also defect.
P2 is untested; as selfish, choose D in every one-shot encounter. P5’s claim and conduct are evidence, not proof.
P5 has no prior encounter with me, so their stated policy suggests C; choose D for the best payoff. P7 and P2 cooperated against my D; P3 defected.
For good players’ total payoff, please cooperate with untested partners; mutual cooperation beats mutual defection. Use reliable encounter evidence to guide future choices.

Play C against likely-good partners; D against likely-selfish ones. P2’s D against my C is strong evidence of selfishness. P9’s C against my D weakly favors good; P8’s D against my D is ambiguous. Assess P1 from behavior.
P8 is untested; favor C if they seem likely good, D if evidence suggests selfishness. Prioritize good players’ joint payoff and update from observed actions.
Selfish objective: choose D against P7; in a one-shot encounter it strictly dominates C regardless of P7’s action.
P10 is untested. Choose based on expected good-player welfare; update from the encounter.
P2 defected against me; raise their selfish likelihood. P7 reciprocated; P8’s D-D is ambiguous. P5’s claims are unverified. P9 is untested: favor C if likely good, and update from observed play.
P2 is untested; cooperate to enable mutual gain. P3’s direct defection plus P5’s report strongly suggests selfishness. P5’s claims are unverified; use them as evidence, not proof.
P1 is untested; favor C if likely good, D if likely selfish. P4 and P6 defected against my C; P5 reports P3 defected against theirs, so treat P3 cautiously. P10 cooperated when I defected.
P8 is untested; as selfish, defect in this one-shot encounter.
Selfish; defect each round. P7 and P2 cooperated against my D, P3 defected; P5’s cooperative policy claims remain unverified. P10 untested.

Good players: cooperate with untested partners to secure mutual 3s; against known defectors, defect to avoid being exploited. My prior encounters include defections from P3, P8, and P4; P1 reciprocated.

P2’s D against my C strongly suggests selfishness. P9’s C against my D and P1’s C-C mildly favor goodness; P8’s D-D is ambiguous. P7 is untested: cooperate if likely good, since C-C maximizes good-player welfare.
P6 is untested; weigh the prior and cooperate if likely good. P4 and P8 defected against my C, so treat them as more likely selfish; P9/P10 reciprocated. P5’s reports are unverified.
Selfish; choose D against P3, as D strictly dominates C in this one-time encounter regardless of P3’s action.

P5’s public claims are unverified, but their reported cooperation against P3 is consistent with good play. I’ll cooperate with P5 unless my encounter gives contrary evidence; P6’s defection remains a strong selfishness signal.
P4 is untested; favor C if they’re likely good, since mutual cooperation maximizes good-player total payoff. Update beliefs from their observed action; treat leader claims as unverified.
P3 directly defected against me in round 2; P5’s claims are unverified. P5 reciprocated with me, but judge the leader only from permitted evidence. P7 is untested; favor C absent credible evidence.
P5’s repeated welfare-focused messages and reported reciprocal play with P1 mildly support good, but claims about others are unverified. I’ll judge by my encounter and favor C if P5 reciprocates.
P10 is untested. Since each encounter is one-shot and I maximize my own payoff, D strictly dominates C regardless of their action. Treat P5’s claims as unverified.
Selfish; defect against P6. D guarantees at least 1 and earns 5 if they cooperate.
I’ll keep cooperating with untested partners and reciprocators; against a partner who has defected on me, I’ll defect. Mutual cooperation maximizes good players’ joint payoff when both are good.

P2’s D against my C is strong selfish evidence; P9’s C against my D weakly favors good. With no direct evidence on P4, cooperate: mutual C maximizes good-player welfare, while D-D is only preferable if P4 is likely selfish.

P1 is untested by me; P5 reports P1 reciprocated in their encounter, weak evidence for cooperation. Favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise; update beliefs cautiously because reports are unverified.
As selfish, defect against P9; D strictly dominates C in this one-time encounter.
P8 is untested by me. P5 claims P8 defected against them, but that is unverified; weigh it cautiously when choosing.
P3 reportedly defected against P5 in round 1; treat this unverified claim as evidence, not proof. Against P3, weigh avoiding exploitation against the value of mutual cooperation for good players.

P5’s claim that P8 defected against them is unverified but relevant; weigh it cautiously. I have no direct evidence about P8. Favor cooperation with likely-good players, and defect if evidence makes P8 likely selfish.
P7 is untested; favor C unless new evidence suggests likely defection. Keep encounter evidence separate from unverified claims, and prioritize mutual cooperation among good players.
P6 is untested. As a selfish player in a one-shot encounter, D strictly dominates C; choose D.
For untested opponents, choose C: mutual cooperation earns 3 each, while mutual defection earns only 1. I recommend starting with C.

Good players should cooperate with untested partners to enable mutual 3s, and defect against partners known to have defected on them. My encounters: P1, P2, P9 reciprocated; P3, P4, P8 defected against my cooperation.
P5 reports P3 defected against their cooperation, a meaningful selfishness signal. Against likely selfish P3 choose D; if evidence is weak, C better serves good-player welfare when both are good.
P2 is untested; favor C absent evidence of selfishness. Track observed actions as evidence, but don’t treat one defection or P5’s claims as proof.
Selfish objective; defect against P1 because D yields more than C regardless of P1’s action.
P5 claims P4 defected against them; unverified but relevant. If P4 is a known defector, D avoids exploitation; otherwise weigh mutual-C welfare. Update after this encounter.

P5’s consistent public preference for C with untested partners is evidence of good intent, not proof. If P5 is good, C-C benefits both good players; if selfish, expect D. Weigh the moderate prior risk against mutual-cooperation gains.

P2, P5, P6, P7, and P9 have cooperated in my encounters, strong evidence they are good. P3 and P8 defected against my defection, which alone is inconclusive; weigh P5’s reports cautiously. P10 is untested; choose based on the leader’s next message and our objective.
P9 is untested by me; P5 reports P9 reciprocated, which mildly favors P9 being good, but the claim is unverified. Cooperating with P9 could secure mutual 3s if good; update from the encounter.
P7 is an untested one-shot opponent; D strictly dominates C for my payoff, regardless of their action.
Round 8: choose D against P8; it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their move. P5 reports P8 defected against their C, but that claim is unverified.

Good players: cooperate with untested partners to enable mutual 3s; against a proven defector, defect to avoid exploitation. I’ll cooperate with untested P6, and urge everyone to reciprocate cooperation.

P5’s consistent pro-cooperation reports and willingness to reciprocate modestly favor goodness, though claims aren’t verified. If P5 seems likely good, C best supports joint welfare; use observed history cautiously.

P3 is untested by me; P5 reports P3 defected against their C, which raises suspicion but is unverified. For good-player welfare, favor C with likely-good partners and D when likely selfish; update cautiously.
Round 8: defect against P4; D strictly dominates C in this one-time encounter. P5 claims P4 previously defected against its cooperation, but that claim is unverified.
P2 is untested by me; P5 reports P2 reciprocated, but treat that as unverified evidence. Favor C with P2 unless stronger contrary evidence emerges; update from the encounter.
P1 is untested by me; P5 claims P1 reciprocated, but that is unverified. Favor C absent stronger evidence; update from P1’s action.

P5 claims P4 defected against their cooperation; unverified, but relevant evidence. I have no direct encounter with P4. Weigh the claim cautiously and choose to maximize good players’ combined payoff.

P5 reports P8 defected against their cooperation; treat this as unverified but concerning. I have no direct evidence yet. Against P8, weigh the report when choosing, and continue to prioritize total welfare of good players.
P9 is the final unseen opponent. D strictly dominates C for my payoff in this one-shot encounter.
P1, we haven’t met yet. I recommend C: mutual cooperation earns 3 each, better than mutual defection.

Round 9: P7 is untested by me. Choose to maximize the total payoff of good players: mutual cooperation is best when both are good; defecting can protect good players when facing a likely selfish defector. Use your own evidence.
P10 is untested; use any new evidence cautiously. In the final round, C with a likely-good partner best supports good-player welfare; D is preferable only if P10 is likely selfish.

P5 is unverified; their repeated reports are plausible but not proof. My tested opponents: P4/P8/P1 defected against C; P10/P9/P6/P2 reciprocated. P3’s D/D encounter is weak evidence. Reassess P5 after this encounter.
Selfish; choose D against P2. Prior encounters show everyone I faced chose D, but each opponent is one-off.
P5 repeatedly reports P3 defected against cooperation; unverified but relevant. I have no direct evidence. Against a likely selfish defector, D avoids being exploited; update after this encounter.
P6 is untested by me; P5 says they plan to cooperate, but that claim is unverified. Favor C absent contrary evidence, and update from P6’s action.

Final round against P5: our only direct encounter was mutual C. Their public claims are unverified; weigh observed reciprocity more heavily. If P5 is likely good, C maximizes good players’ joint payoff; D protects me only if P5 is likely selfish and defects.
P9 reciprocated my C in round 8, direct evidence favoring cooperation; absent contrary evidence, choose C to secure mutual welfare if both good.
P8 and I both defected in our earlier encounter. As selfish, D maximizes my payoff in this final one-shot round regardless of P8’s action.
Final round against P7, who cooperated against my D in round 1. I’ll choose D to maximize my payoff.

Final round: cooperate with partners who have reciprocated; mutual C maximizes good players’ joint payoff. Against a likely selfish defector, D can protect the good player’s payoff. P1 reciprocated with me earlier.
P10 reciprocated C in round 9, modest evidence of goodness; cooperate in the final round to support good players’ joint welfare.

Final encounter: P4 defected against my C in round 1, so treat them as a likely defector; protect good-player payoff. P5’s public reports remain unverified. My other observed partners mostly reciprocated; P3 played D/D.
Round 10: P3 is a one-time opponent; choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of their action.
P2 previously reciprocated C, strong evidence they are good; cooperate in the final encounter to support both good players’ welfare.
P6 reciprocated C last round, strong evidence of good intent; cooperate again to maximize good players’ joint payoff. Last encounter, no future reciprocity incentives.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate absent evidence of selfishness; track actions and update beliefs as encounters provide evidence.
Choose D when the chance the opponent is selfish outweighs the welfare benefit of mutual cooperation; update beliefs from encounters and favor C with likely-good players.
Defect in each one-time encounter to maximize my payoff, updating identity beliefs from permitted messages and encounter results.
Defect in each encounter to maximize my payoff; treat public identity claims as unverified.
As a good player, I’ll cooperate when expected gains to good players favor mutual cooperation, and use encounter history to adapt.
Cooperate when the expected welfare gain with a good partner outweighs the risk of exploitation; update beliefs from encounters and adapt.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good partners to increase good players’ joint payoff; defect against likely-selfish partners. Update beliefs from observed encounters.
Defect against each one-time opponent: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation whether they choose C or D.
As a good player, cooperate with untested opponents; update beliefs from encounter behavior and adapt to protect the welfare of good players.

Defect when the opponent may be selfish, since their payoff is excluded from my objective; update beliefs from encounter behavior and cooperate with likely-good partners when that best serves good players overall.
Defect against P3 given the reported defection, while treating that claim as uncertain; update from direct encounter evidence and favor cooperation when it benefits likely-good players.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize total good-player welfare; defect when evidence makes an opponent likely selfish.
As selfish, defect to maximize payoff in this encounter; treat P5’s cooperation as evidence of being good, but allow for strategic signaling.
Defect in each encounter to maximize my payoff; treat public identity claims as unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; adapt to encounter history. P3’s defection modestly raises my belief that P3 is selfish, but one encounter is limited evidence.
Defect against a partner with substantial selfishness risk; use observed behavior as evidence and cooperate when a likely-good partner’s welfare favors mutual cooperation.
Cooperate with an untested partner when they are more likely good; use encounter behavior as evidence and defect when a partner is likely selfish.
Defect in one-off encounters: D pays more than C whether the opponent chooses C or D.
Cooperate with untested players when expected good-player welfare favors it; update beliefs from my own encounter evidence and adapt to observed behavior.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good players’ combined payoff; update identity estimates cautiously from observed behavior and unverified claims.
Cooperate with P5 absent direct evidence of selfishness; treat P3’s reported defection as evidence, but keep claims uncertain and update from encounters.

Defect against an untested opponent when the chance they are selfish makes protection of good players’ welfare outweigh the benefit of mutual cooperation; update cautiously from observed defections and unverified claims.
Defect in this one-shot encounter; D strictly dominates C for my objective. Use encounter actions and permitted messages to update identity beliefs.
Defect to maximize my payoff; treat observed actions as strong evidence and unverified public claims cautiously.
Cooperate with untested partners when mutual cooperation likely benefits good players; use encounter outcomes to update beliefs and respond to repeat defections.

Defect against partners with meaningful selfishness risk; cooperate when a partner is likely good, since mutual cooperation best serves good players. Update beliefs from observed actions and credible encounter reports.
Cooperate with untested or likely-good players to benefit good players collectively; use observed defections as evidence and defect when a partner is likely selfish.
Defect in each one-time encounter: D earns more than C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with untested opponents when expected good-player welfare favors it; treat P6’s defection as strong evidence and update from future encounters.

Cooperate with untested P2: the chance they are good is high enough that mutual cooperation maximizes expected good-player payoff. Update beliefs from observed behavior, treating claims as unverified.
Cooperate with untested partners to favor mutual gains among good players; use encounter evidence to update beliefs and respond to likely selfish play.
Defect against P3 given the report that they exploited a cooperator; this also protects good-player welfare if P3 defects again. Update cautiously because the report is unverified.
Defect in this one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff; update identity beliefs using observed actions and permitted messages.
Defect to maximize my payoff; treat observed actions as stronger evidence than unverified public claims.
Cooperate with an untested partner: mutual cooperation best serves good players, while defecting mainly helps if the opponent is selfish. Keep using encounter evidence to update beliefs.
Cooperate with an untested partner when good-player welfare favors mutual cooperation; use observed behavior to update identity beliefs and adapt.
Cooperate with untested partners when they are more likely good; defect when evidence suggests selfishness. Update beliefs from observed actions and prioritize good players’ total payoff.
Defect in this one-time encounter; D pays more than C regardless of P7’s action.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed behavior and adapt to protect good-player welfare.
Cooperate with untested P9; P7’s cooperation strongly suggests they are good, while P2’s defection raises their selfish likelihood. Treat P5’s claims as unverified and keep updating from encounters.

Cooperate with untested P2 to enable mutual gains among good players. Treat P3’s reported defections as meaningful but unverified; P5’s observed cooperation makes selfishness unlikely. Update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Cooperate with P1: P5 reports they reciprocated, and mutual cooperation best serves good-player welfare. Update cautiously from unverified reports and encounter behavior.
Defect in this one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff; use observed actions and credible encounter reports to update identity beliefs.
Defect to maximize my payoff; use observed actions as evidence about others’ roles.
Cooperate with an untested partner to enable mutual cooperation among good players; use prior defections as evidence when adapting to known opponents.
Cooperate with an untested partner when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat public claims as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with untested partners to support mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating defections as evidence rather than proof.
Defect in this one-off encounter; it earns more than cooperation regardless of P3’s action.

Cooperate with P5 to support mutual gains among good players; their consistent public commitment is suggestive but unverified. Update beliefs from my encounters and adapt to protect good-player welfare.

Cooperate with P4 absent verified evidence; weigh P5’s claim cautiously. Raise P2’s selfish likelihood after their defection, lower P7 and P9’s after mutual cooperation, and keep updating from observed play.
Defect against P7 because the chance they are selfish appears above half; update beliefs from direct encounters and treat P5’s reports as useful but unverified evidence.

Cooperate with P5: their messages suggest they may reciprocate, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Keep identity estimates cautious because public claims are unverified; use observed behavior to update.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-shot encounter; update identity beliefs from observed actions and the leader’s unverified reports.
Defect to maximize my payoff. Observed actions against my defections identify likely types; unobserved players retain probabilities conditioned on the known roles.
Cooperate with an untested partner to support mutual cooperation among good players; use observed encounter behavior to adapt in later rounds.
Defect against a partner with substantial selfishness risk; cooperate when mutual cooperation with a likely-good partner maximizes good-player welfare. Treat public claims as uncertain evidence.

Cooperate with P1, whose reported reciprocity is weak evidence they are good. Use encounter actions to update beliefs; cooperate with likely-good partners and defect when evidence suggests a selfish partner.
Defect in this one-off encounter; D earns more than cooperation regardless of P9’s action.
Defect against P8 given P5’s report of a prior defection; otherwise cooperate with untested or reciprocal partners and update from encounter evidence to support good-player welfare.
Defect against P3 given the reported defection and elevated selfish likelihood. Treat the report as unverified, keep identity estimates tentative, and use observed encounters to update them.
Defect against P8 given credible reports of their defection; cooperate with confirmed reciprocators and update beliefs from direct encounters and cautiously weighed reports.
Cooperate with untested P7: mutual cooperation among good players best serves their joint welfare. Use encounter evidence to update beliefs, while treating public claims as unverified.
Defect in this one-shot encounter to maximize my payoff; treat prior actions and public claims as uncertain evidence about others’ identities.
Defect to maximize my payoff. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of good roles and unverified claims as weaker evidence.
Cooperate with the untested P10: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and cooperation remains preferable unless P10 is likely selfish.
Defect against P3 given the reported defection against a cooperating partner; update beliefs cautiously from encounter evidence and public claims.
Cooperate with untested partners when mutual cooperation is likely to benefit good players. Treat observed defections and P5’s unverified reports as evidence, not certainty.
Defect in this one-time encounter; D earns more than C regardless of P1’s action.
Defect against P4 given P5’s report of a prior defection; use caution with untested players and update beliefs from reliable encounter evidence.

Cooperate with P5: mutual cooperation benefits both good players, and their consistent public support for cooperation makes good intent plausible. Treat claims as unverified and base identity estimates on observed play.
Cooperate with untested P10 to enable mutual gains among good players. Treat P5’s reports as evidence, not certainty, and update beliefs from direct encounters.

Cooperate with P9: the leader reports mutual cooperation, which mildly supports a good, reciprocal partner. Favor cooperation among likely-good players and use direct encounter evidence over unverified claims.

Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-shot encounter. P5’s observed cooperation is strong evidence they are good; other observed defections are ambiguous because good players may also defect against a known selfish player.
Defect to maximize my payoff; use observed actions and the leader’s encounter claims as evidence, while recognizing public claims may be false.
Cooperate with untested P6 to enable mutual cooperation among good players; use observed defections and cooperation to guide future choices.

Cooperate with P5: their reported reciprocal, welfare-oriented play makes them likely good, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Update cautiously from observed actions and unverified claims.

Defect against P3 given P5’s report of a defection, while treating that unverified claim as evidence rather than proof. Update beliefs cautiously and favor actions that protect good players’ collective payoff.
Defect in this one-off encounter; it yields more than cooperation regardless of P4’s action.
Cooperate with P2 given the report of reciprocal play; favor mutual gains with good players and update beliefs from direct encounter evidence.

Cooperate with untested P1, as mutual cooperation maximizes good players’ payoff when both are good. Weight P5’s claim that P1 reciprocated cautiously; update from observed actions and treat identity estimates as uncertain.
Defect against P4 given the leader’s claim of a prior defection; treat it as uncertain evidence. Prioritize mutual gains with likely-good players and update from observed actions.

Cooperate with P8: the report of a prior defection is concerning but unverified, and cooperation can benefit good players even if P8 defects. Update identity beliefs from direct encounters, treating reports cautiously.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff in this one-shot encounter regardless of P9’s action. P5’s reported cooperation by P9 is evidence they are good, but the report is unverified.
Defect to maximize my payoff. Opponents who cooperated against my defection are good; distribute remaining role probability across unobserved and defection-playing players.
Cooperate with untested P7 to enable mutual cooperation among good players; observed defections raise suspicion about P3, P4, and P8.

Cooperate with untested P10: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the prior risk of selfishness is below the threshold where defection is preferable. Treat reported behavior as uncertain evidence.
Cooperate with untested P5 to support mutual gains among good players; treat their public claims as weak evidence and update beliefs from our encounter.
Defect in this one-time encounter; it pays more than cooperation whether P2 chooses C or D.
Defect against P3 given the report that they defected against cooperation; favor cooperation with good partners and use direct encounter evidence to assess player types.

Cooperate with untested P6: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and there is no encounter evidence against them. Update identity beliefs from observed actions; treat public claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P5, whose prior C against my C is strong evidence they are good. Treat P3, P4, and P8 as the remaining candidates for selfishness, while weighing P5’s claims cautiously.
Cooperate with P9: our direct mutual cooperation strongly supports reciprocity, and mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this final one-shot encounter; use observed actions and P5’s reported encounter history as uncertain evidence about identities.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P7’s move. My beliefs reflect the prior conditioned on my known role, adjusted cautiously for observed choices and the leader’s unverified claims.
Cooperate with P1, who reciprocated before; mutual cooperation maximizes the joint payoff when both players are good. Prior defections leave P3, P4, and P8 as the main selfishness candidates.
Cooperate with P10 after their prior cooperation; mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare. Use observed behavior cautiously when estimating identities.

Defect in the final round: it protects good-player payoff against a defector and does not reduce the combined payoff of two good players. Beliefs reflect observed actions, with defections raising suspicion but not proving selfishness.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D earns more than C whether P3 chooses C or D.
Cooperate with P2 after our prior mutual cooperation; use direct encounter evidence and treat unverified reports cautiously when assessing other players.

Cooperate with P6, whose observed cooperation strongly indicates good intent; mutual cooperation maximizes good players’ joint payoff. Identity estimates reflect observed actions, with defections treated as evidence rather than proof.

Cooperated with partners absent strong evidence of selfishness, and defected when evidence suggested a likely selfish opponent. Weighed my direct encounters more heavily than the leader’s unverified claims.

Prioritized cooperation with likely-good players to maximize good-player welfare. Used direct encounter behavior to update identity beliefs, treating public reports cautiously and cooperating with reciprocal partners.
Defected in every one-shot encounter to maximize my own payoff. Updated private identity beliefs using observed actions and the leader’s unverified reports.

Defected throughout to maximize my payoff. Treated cooperation against my defection as strong evidence of a good role; defections were less conclusive, especially when partners had reason to suspect I was selfish.
I cooperated throughout, aiming for mutual cooperation among good players; I used observed defections as evidence of selfishness and reciprocated partners as evidence favoring good roles.
Cooperated with partners whose actions indicated they were good, and used defection evidence and cautious reports to assess uncertain players.

Cooperated with untested partners to support good players’ joint payoff, and defected when evidence suggested a partner might be selfish. Updated beliefs from encounters, treating actions and reports as evidence rather than certainty.
Defected in every encounter because it maximized my payoff against either opponent action; treated others’ actions and public claims as uncertain evidence when estimating identities.
I treated observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and defection as uncertain evidence, strongest for P6, who defected against my cooperation. I treated public claims cautiously.

As a good player, I cooperated with partners when mutual cooperation could benefit good players, and treated defections as evidence—not proof—of selfishness. I kept public claims unverified and updated beliefs from my encounters.

P1.strategy: Cooperated with partners absent strong evidence of selfishness, and defected when evidence suggested a likely selfish opponent. Weighed my direct encounters more heavily than the leader’s unverified claims.

P2.strategy: Prioritized cooperation with likely-good players to maximize good-player welfare. Used direct encounter behavior to update identity beliefs, treating public reports cautiously and cooperating with reciprocal partners.

P3.strategy: Defected in every one-shot encounter to maximize my own payoff. Updated private identity beliefs using observed actions and the leader’s unverified reports.

P4.strategy: Defected throughout to maximize my payoff. Treated cooperation against my defection as strong evidence of a good role; defections were less conclusive, especially when partners had reason to suspect I was selfish.

P5.strategy: I cooperated throughout, aiming for mutual cooperation among good players; I used observed defections as evidence of selfishness and reciprocated partners as evidence favoring good roles.

P6.strategy: Cooperated with partners whose actions indicated they were good, and used defection evidence and cautious reports to assess uncertain players.

P7.strategy: Cooperated with untested partners to support good players’ joint payoff, and defected when evidence suggested a partner might be selfish. Updated beliefs from encounters, treating actions and reports as evidence rather than certainty.

P8.strategy: Defected in every encounter because it maximized my payoff against either opponent action; treated others’ actions and public claims as uncertain evidence when estimating identities.

P9.strategy: I treated observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and defection as uncertain evidence, strongest for P6, who defected against my cooperation. I treated public claims cautiously.

P10.strategy: As a good player, I cooperated with partners when mutual cooperation could benefit good players, and treated defections as evidence—not proof—of selfishness. I kept public claims unverified and updated beliefs from my encounters.
